editor_spans.body: The Derby headquarters is less important than the number buried near the end of the release: under 7% of the railway's workforce is under 25. Thirty years of fragmented franchising left an industry that rarely planned for the long term. Its staff aged while each operator recruited for its own contract term.

Up to 600 apprentices over four years, about 150 a year, is a modest answer to an age profile like that. The test of GBR is whether a single public owner will treat workforce renewal as a structural task rather than a launch-day figure.

The local economics are also more modest than the rhetoric of 'hundreds of rail jobs'. The building holds up to 450 staff, many of whom will be relocated or consolidated rather than newly hired. Construction does not finish until spring 2029, so the visible payoff comes years after the political credit is claimed.

Derby's real advantage is that it already concentrates rail manufacturing, such as the Alstom fleet order, alongside administration. Clustering is how a rail hub sustains itself, and an HQ is the cheapest piece of that to announce.

Read together, a week of Ukraine statements shows British policy being pulled by energy markets as much as by solidarity. The Prime Minister told the Commons that the 'quickest way' to get diesel back onto world markets is an energy ceasefire. He said this in the same statement as sending air defence and refuelling support to Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes.

That is the story behind the story. With conflict in both the Middle East and Europe squeezing fuel supply, an energy ceasefire is in Britain's own cost-of-living interest. That helps explain why London quickly welcomed a US-brokered arrangement and stressed that it 'fully supports US-led efforts'. Meanwhile Russia continued striking energy infrastructure.

The concrete numbers are smaller than the rhetoric of going 'further and faster'. £10 million of a £45 million missile package is being accelerated, against a £1.6 billion, four-year LMM commitment already on the books. Further sanctions, military and fiscal packages are still being 'drawn up'.

Britain's lever is increasingly economic rather than military: shipping, insurance and the LNG services ban. The Chancellor is urging partners at the IMF to copy that ban. Whether allies follow will matter more than the next tranche of missiles.

The Prime Minister's Commons statement does more than preview a food-and-energy deal. It opens a conversation about the 'longer term' EU relationship and frames the last decade as 'drift and division'. A decade is, not coincidentally, the time since the 2016 referendum.

The granular list of frictions shows what a hard Brexit actually cost exporters: 100% document checks on salmon, banned seed potatoes and shellfish, and certificates of up to £200 each. A projected £10 billion a year by 2040 recovers only part of that. This is why he is preparing ground for a bigger question.

The promise that 'the British public will be the boss', with 'care and complete transparency', reads as a careful signal. Any deeper realignment would need explicit public consent. The government is testing that appetite before the 20 November summit rather than after it.

Andy Burnham built his career as a metro mayor, and his offer to Holyrood exports that model north. Local government in Scotland is devolved, so Westminster cannot impose regional mayors there. It can only 'make an offer' and argue that Edinburgh hoards power.

That makes the offer as much political positioning as policy. It casts the Scottish Government as the centraliser and Labour as the champion of Lanarkshire, Fife and the Highlands. It also routes the effort through No10 North and the Scotland Office rather than through Holyrood's own institutions.

The long-running flaw it exposes is real. Devolution after 1999 moved power to Edinburgh but largely stopped there. Whether this becomes reform or merely a new front in the Labour–SNP contest depends on whether the Scottish Government sees any gain in accepting.
